appraisal_events.evidence: "Il leur fit au contraire une excellente impression dont à leur insu sa fréquentation dans la société élégante était une des causes indirectes"; his ease with the Verdurins, 'gens d'un milieu inférieur au sien,' is described as instinctive advances 'dont selon eux un ennuyeux se fût abstenu.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator explains that Swann's polish and ease, acquired from moving in elite society, make an unexpectedly excellent impression on the socially inferior Verdurin circle, elevating him locally even though the Verdurins themselves do not grasp the source of his grace.

appraisal_events.evidence: Cottard reacts to Swann's mere name 'd'un accent rendu brutal par la surprise... cet homme qui se croyait perpétuellement préparé à tout'; later he interrupts Swann 'd'un air moqueur' and finishes his sentence with an ironic cliché, though the narrator notes Swann 'n'y avait jamais pensé.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator frames Cottard as socially maladroit across the passage: he is comically caught off guard despite believing himself always prepared, and he closes the scene by reflexively and groundlessly mocking Swann's sincere remark, a misjudgment the narrator explicitly flags as unfounded.

status_effects.explanation: Swann's worldly ease gives him unexpectedly high local standing among the Verdurin circle, who had feared he would be a bore.
Cottard is cast in a locally unflattering light through his anxious overreaction to a name and his unwarranted, reflexive mockery of Swann's earnest remark.

ambiguities: Cottard's closing mockery of Swann's phrase can be read either as narrator-led exposure of Cottard's own social tic (as annotated here) or, less centrally, as a momentary public snub of Swann; the passage's explicit clarification that Swann 'n'y avait jamais pensé' supports reading it primarily as diminishing Cottard's judgment rather than Swann's standing.
